question: The unchecked proliferation of wind and solar photovoltaic plants is radically altering the landscapes and economic fabric of the Belice area – a rural region in western Sicily that relies heavily on agriculture – while also harming its producers.

Meeting in Castelvetrano, local mayors criticised what they view as an energy transition model which has been imposed from on high and which benefits large industrial groups at the expense of the Belice area’s communities and identity.

While the number of requests to connect installations to the electricity grid is already four times higher than planned, the areas deemed unsuitable for renewable energy plants have yet to be mapped out, even though such a measure was provided for by the Legislative Decree (No 199/2021) that transposed Directive (EU) 2018/2001 (known as RED II).

This state of affairs could also jeopardise the investments made to protect and develop rural areas under both the Common Agricultural Policy and the European Agricultural Fund for Rural Development. In the light of the above: 1.
Could the Commission clarify whether this state of affairs is in line with CAP and territorial cohesion objectives?
Is this state of affairs compatible with the principles of the EU Green Deal, and does it respect territorial specificities?

Which instruments will the Commission use to ensure that the environmental transition is not used as a pretext to cause further environmental and economic disruption in the EU’s rural and inland areas?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (19.9.2025) The deployment of renewable energy can create opportunities for farmers and rural areas. In a context of competition for land-use, it is important to combine it with the need to value appropriately ecosystem services and to ensure business models that retain value within rural communities.

While the promotion of sustainable energy is part of the specific objectives of the Common Agricultural Policy (CAP), it is up to the Member State to make detailed implementation decisions in their CAP strategic plans, depending on national specificities and needs.

To achieve its 2030 energy objectives, and to deliver secure and affordable energy to European citizens and companies, the EU must accelerate the deployment of renewables, with wind and solar playing a major role.

While the deployment of renewables is subject to decisions of competent authorities in the Member States, it is not incompatible with protecting biodiversity and safeguarding farmers’ livelihoods, which can be simultaneously promoted. Farmers are among those most affected by climate change, and the roll out of renewables is fundamental to mitigate its effects.

The revised Renewable Energy Directive1 mandates Member States to designate renewables acceleration areas particularly suitable for renewable energy projects, which will benefit from short permitting procedures, with an emphasis on prioritising areas that are not usable for agriculture such as industrial zones.

Furthermore, to minimise land use and encourage multiple use of space - including combining renewables deployment and agriculture - the Commission has issued recommendations and guidance for Member States on encouraging innovative technologies and forms of renewable energy deployment2, such as agrivoltaics.
1 Directive (EU) 2018/2001 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 11 December 2018 on the
promotion of the use of energy from renewable sources (OJ L 328, 21.12.2018, p. 82, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/dir/2018/2001/oj. 2 C(2025) 4024 final and C(2025) 4011 final, respectively.
